# `sysctl_setting`

A Kubernetes node, a router, or a busy file watcher needs kernel settings
that differ from the defaults. `sysctl_setting` manages one kernel setting:
the value that `sysctl` shows and the kernel keeps under `/proc/sys`. MMX
sets the value now, and keeps it for the next boot in its own file,
`/etc/sysctl.d/90-mmx-<name>.conf`.

A setting that a kernel module adds exists only while that module is
loaded; [`kernel_module`](kernel_module.md) loads it.

## Inputs

- `name` (string; required): as sysctl writes it, such as net.ipv4.ip_forward; when a part has a dot in it, such as the interface eth0.10, write slashes between all the parts: net/ipv4/conf/eth0.10/rp_filter. A name the kernel does not have fails the task before any change
- `value` (string; required): the value as sysctl shows it, such as "1"; compared word by word, so "32768 60999" matches the kernel's tab; a value the kernel refuses fails the task with its message; omit with boot_setting_removed_live_value_kept
- `state` (`present` or `boot_setting_removed_live_value_kept`; default `present`): boot_setting_removed_live_value_kept deletes MMX's configuration file and accepts only name; the current kernel value stays until boot-time configuration is applied at the next boot

## Outputs

The node task's result holds these fields. A later node task reads them as `.node_tasks.<id>.<field>`, where `<id>` is the node task's `id`.

- `status`
- `change`
- `value.live_value_before`
- `value.live_value_after`

## What a dryrun reports

Supported; reports the old and the new live value and the difference of MMX's file; a name the kernel does not have yet is not checked, because an earlier kernel_module task may add it. A file applied at boot after MMX's that sets the setting to another value fails the task, in a dryrun too.

## Retries and time limits

Bounded automatic retries by default; retry: false turns them off.

The node task takes the time limits `time_limit` and `time_limit_per_try`; without them, the project's `node_task_defaults` apply. `mmx describe-module task` describes the settings every node task accepts.

## Examples

### Settings for a Kubernetes node

```yaml
- kernel_module:
    name: br_netfilter

- id: kernel_settings
  loop:
    net.ipv4.ip_forward: "1"
    net.bridge.bridge-nf-call-iptables: "1"
    fs.inotify.max_user_instances: "1048576"
  as: setting
  sysctl_setting:
    name: "{{ .setting.key }}"
    value: "{{ .setting.value }}"
```

The first node task loads the kernel module `br_netfilter` on the node now
and at every boot. The loop then sets three kernel settings, one node task
for each. The second setting exists only while `br_netfilter` is loaded,
which is why the `kernel_module` node task comes first.

### A setting of a VLAN interface

```yaml
- sysctl_setting:
    name: net/ipv4/conf/eth0.10/rp_filter
    value: "2"
```

A name that has a part with a dot in it, such as the VLAN interface
`eth0.10`, is written with slashes between all its parts. MMX keeps the
setting's name and value in `90-mmx-net.ipv4.conf.eth0.10.rp_filter.conf`.
A name with slashes gets dots in the file name.

### Remove MMX's file

```yaml
- sysctl_setting:
    name: fs.inotify.max_user_instances
    state: boot_setting_removed_live_value_kept
```

`state: boot_setting_removed_live_value_kept` takes only `name` and deletes MMX's file. The live value
stays as it is, because MMX does not know the value the node would have
without the file; the next boot decides it.

## How it works

- `name` is written as `sysctl` writes it, such as `net.ipv4.ip_forward`.
- `value` is text, as `sysctl` shows it; quote a number, such as `"1"`. MMX
  compares values word by word, so `"32768 60999"` matches the kernel's
  `32768	60999`, which has a tab.
- MMX reads the live value from `/proc/sys`. When the live value differs
  from `value`, MMX writes `value` to the setting's file under `/proc/sys`
  and reports `value.live_value_before` and `value.live_value_after`.
- Only the kernel setting in `name` is applied: MMX does not restart
  `systemd-sysctl.service`, which would apply every setting file again.
- For the next boot, MMX keeps the setting in its own file,
  `/etc/sysctl.d/90-mmx-<name>.conf`, which holds one line, such as
  `net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1`.
- The module needs nothing installed beyond what the tested distributions have.
- A dryrun reports the old and the new value. A name the kernel does not
  have yet is not checked in a dryrun, because an earlier `kernel_module`
  node task may add it.

### Which file wins at boot

At boot, `systemd-sysctl` applies the `.conf` files of `/etc/sysctl.d/`,
`/run/sysctl.d/`, `/usr/local/lib/sysctl.d/`, and `/usr/lib/sysctl.d/`. A
file in an earlier directory of that list hides a file of the same name in a
later one; that is how a link to `/dev/null` in `/etc/sysctl.d/` switches a
vendor file off. The remaining files apply in the order of their names,
whatever their directory, and the last value of a setting wins.

`sysctl --system` reads the same files and then `/etc/sysctl.conf`. Every tested distribution except Debian 13 also links that file
into `/etc/sysctl.d/` as `99-sysctl.conf`, so `systemd-sysctl` reads it
there too. MMX therefore counts `/etc/sysctl.conf` as the last file
everywhere.

When a file that comes after MMX's sets the same setting to another value,
the node task fails and names that file, because the node would boot with
the other value; in a dryrun too. A pattern such as
`net.ipv4.conf.*.rp_filter` in a later file does not count:
`systemd-sysctl` lets a named setting win over a pattern.

## Errors and what they mean

A failure that another try cannot fix is not tried again: a refused value,
or a later file that assigns a conflicting value to the requested kernel
setting.

| The reason holds | What the error means, and what to do |
|---|---|
| `the kernel has no setting ... (... does not exist); check the setting name, or add a kernel_module task before the sysctl_setting task to load the kernel module that provides the setting` | A name the kernel does not have fails the node task before any change, so a misspelled name is never kept in a file that the kernel ignores. Check the spelling, or load the kernel module first. |
| `the kernel refused ... = ...: ...` | The kernel refused the value, such as a setting that a container may not change. The reason ends with the kernel's message, and MMX's file keeps its old line. |
| `... sets the managed kernel setting to ... after MMX's file ... is applied, so the node would boot with ...; remove the conflicting kernel setting from ..., or manage the kernel setting in the conflicting file instead of with MMX` | A later file sets the setting to another value; see [Which file wins at boot](#which-file-wins-at-boot). Remove the line from that file, or set the value there instead of with MMX. |

## Tested on

**Distributions:** Debian 12 and 13, Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Rocky Linux 9, AlmaLinux 10.

The suite `tests/integration/kernel_settings.py` runs in virtual machines
with Debian 12 and 13, Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, Rocky Linux 9, and AlmaLinux 10. Virtual machines are needed because kernel settings belong to the
kernel, which a container shares with the container's host.
The suite `tests/integration/kernel_settings.py` checks the values in
`/proc/sys` and runs `systemd-sysctl` as the next boot runs `systemd-sysctl`.
The [validation record](../../changing-mmx/validation.md) has the latest results.

## Why it works this way

- **`sysctl_setting`, not a file in `/etc/sysctl.d/` with a restart of
  `systemd-sysctl.service`.** Kernel settings are common in real projects:
  46 independent authors set them in the Ansible projects MMX was checked
  against. With a `file` node task and a restart of
  `systemd-sysctl.service`, MMX reports only the file's difference.
  The `file` node task silently keeps misspelled setting names, and the
  service restart applies every setting file again. `sysctl_setting`
  compares the live value, refuses a name the kernel does not have, and
  applies only the requested kernel setting.
- **A later file fails the task.** The node would otherwise boot with
  another value than the one the run reported.
- **`state: boot_setting_removed_live_value_kept` leaves the live value alone.**
  MMX does not know the value the node would have without
  `/etc/sysctl.d/90-mmx-<name>.conf`.
